name: Ma'di
confidence_why: Blackings and Fabb's 2003 reference grammar found no syllable of any Ma'di word that predictably carries stronger stress and explicitly rejected the final-syllable stress reported in Tucker and Bryan's 1966 survey, whose brief four-example note is the only source on the other side, while Kilpatrick 1985 and Tucker 1940 describe tone only and say nothing about stress.

catalog_quote: 3.5.5. Absence of stress We have not found evidence that, for any Ma'di word, a particular syllable predictably carries stronger stress than any other syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ma'di is a three-level tone language (H, M, L); the reference grammar finds no syllable in any word that predictably bears greater stress than the others and explicitly rejects Tucker & Bryan's (1966: 31) claim, which reads (verbatim from the 1966 handbook): 'In MA'DI, however, stress is on the final vowel: i'za, lé'dra, a'ri, lé'ndri' (contrasted there with initial stress in closely related Moru). So: modern primary description = no predictable word stress; older handbook = fixed final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned in the accessible text.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (pp. 40, 68): their tonal patterns mimic the stressed syllable of the source word (e.g. Juba Arabic), e.g. bisyllables have HL tone if and only if they are loanwords; a few words vary in tone. This is tone reflecting foreign stress, not native stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word ('for any Ma'di word'); the continuation of the second sentence and any remarks on phrase-level prominence lie beyond the snippet (full text paywalled). Grammar is based chiefly on co-author Blackings' own Lokai ('Uganda') Ma'di.
new_statements.identity_note: Blackings & Fabb 2003 describe Ma'di [mhi, madi1260] chiefly on the basis of co-author Mairi John Blackings' own speech, the Lokai ('Ugandan') dialect (Fabb's Sentence Structure workbook states Blackings 'speaks the Lokai dialect of Madi'); Kilpatrick 1985 describes Lokai as spoken on the Sudan side; Tucker & Bryan's MA'DI rests on Tucker's 1940 Lokai and Pandikeri data. All are madi1260. Caution: the sil.org 'Ma'di Uruleti' (Okollo) materials are Southern Ma'di [snm, sout2828], a different Glottolog language, and 'Madi [grg]' on sil.org is a Papua New Guinea language; neither was used for the statement.

new_statements.quote: No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words, even when it is a vowel Prefix, e.g. 'iza, meat; after a consonant there is a tendency to lengthen the vowel [...] In MA'DI, however, stress is on the final vowel: i'za, lé'dra, a'ri, lé'ndrì. In both languages words within a phrase retain their original stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's existing statement (Blackings & Fabb 2003: 42, sec. 3.5.5 'Absence of stress', page scan read: 'We have not found evidence that, for any Ma'di word, a particular syllable predictably carries stronger stress than any other syllable. We therefore do not support Tucker and Bryan's (1966: 31) claim that stress is basically iambic (eg. final stress on a disyllable).') records no word stress; Tucker & Bryan assert fixed final stress. Different type (fixed: final syllable vs no word stress). This is exactly the claim Blackings & Fabb examined and rejected.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Ma'di, stress falls on the final vowel (last syllable) of the word, explicitly contrasted with Moru, where stress is on the first syllable of disyllables; word stress is kept when the word stands inside a phrase. Examples in the 1966 printing: i'za 'meat', lé'dra 'tongue', a'ri 'bird', lé'ndrì 'shadow' (all disyllables; nothing said about longer words).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ma'di. The section is a short comparative note: the Ma'di statement rests on four disyllabic examples; the 2017 reprint page scan re-sets the example line with the stress marks in different places ('léndrì, 'léndr, i'za, lè'dra), while the 1966 scanned reads i'za, lé'dra, a'ri, lé'ndrì; the prose sentence 'stress is on the final vowel' is identical in both. The same section reports stress on the penultimate syllable for Mangbetu (Larochette) and initial stress for Moru.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's MA'DI and Tucker 1940's Madi (Pandikeri, Lulu'ba) are the Moru-Ma'di language of South Sudan/Uganda = madi1260, not Southern Ma'di [snm] (sout2828); Glottolog's assignment of Andersen 1986 to Southern Ma'di is an autotranslation artefact. Blackings & Fabb 2003 describe Uganda Ma'di; Kilpatrick 1985 (already held by the project, no stress statement) describes the Lokai dialect of the Sudan side.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Tucker 1940/1967 (index 2) does contain the word 'stress' once, in the Introduction, II. Linguistic, sec. 268 (a numbered list of Hamitic/Semitic characteristics, following 'ablaut' at 267 and preceding 'Characteristic consonant sounds of both Hamitic and Semitic languages' at 269): '268. 4. Dynamic accent (stress) plays a greater role than tone in differentiating words.' Print page not recoverable from the snippet (the Introduction's linguistic section runs to about p. 68-88 of vol. I). It characterises Hamitic/Semitic languages, not Ma'di, so the work stays silent for madi1260; but the compiler statement that the token 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the item's scanned is wrong.

readall_conflicts: Tucker & Bryan (1966: 31) state that in Ma'di 'stress is on the final vowel' (fixed: final syllable, four disyllabic examples, contrasted with initial stress in Moru), whereas the catalog's existing statement from Blackings & Fabb (2003: 42, sec. 3.5.5 'Absence of stress') says no syllable of any Ma'di word predictably carries stronger stress and explicitly rejects Tucker & Bryan's 'basically iambic' claim. The two sources disagree on type (fixed final stress vs no word stress). Tucker 1940 is silent (tone only) and Andersen 1986 could not be opened, so nothing else settles; the full modern grammar, which examined the older claim directly, is the better-supported reading.
